Models propose. Yana decides. Humans stay in charge.

A local control plane that sits between any AI model and real power over your machine.

English · Tiếng Việt · 한국어 · 中文

Quick start · How it works · Yana Studio · Performance · Limits · Website

Counts are derived from the filesystem by core/scripts/check_counts.py, which CI runs. Timings are local measurements from 2026-10-20; the method is under Performance.

Quick start

Desktop app. Download Yana Studio from the latest release or yana.vutam.link.

Platform Installer
macOS, Apple Silicon .dmg or .zip
Windows .exe, x64 or ARM64
Linux, x86_64 .deb or .AppImage

Command line. Govern the agent you already use:

pip install yana-ai    # Python CLI
yana-ai install        # add Yana's hooks and rules to your repo
yana-ai doctor .       # check that everything is wired
cargo install yana-rt  # native runtime, no Python needed

Needs Python 3.11+ (or Rust), Git, and one supported host. All CLI commands are in COMMANDS.md. Yana is not published to npm, see VERSIONING.md.

Note

The macOS build is ad-hoc signed and not notarized (no Apple Developer membership yet), so Gatekeeper warns on first launch. docs/MACOS_INSTALL.md shows the two official ways to open it. Each release lists its own assets: check that your platform is there and verify against SHA256SUMS when provided. There is no Linux ARM build.

How it works

A model can say what it wants to do. Yana decides whether that is allowed, and a person can always stop it. Every model takes the same path: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, or one running on your own machine.

flowchart LR
    M["Model<br/>proposes an action"] --> A["Authority<br/>may this agent ask?"]
    A --> C["Capability<br/>which exact power?"]
    C --> P["Policy<br/>rules first, then a human"]
    P -->|allowed| E["Executor<br/>runs only that operation"]
    P -->|denied| X["Blocked<br/>with a reason"]
    E --> L[("Hash-chained<br/>audit log")]
    X --> L
Loading

Skills teach an agent how to work. Only a capability can grant permission to act.

System structure

Component What it does Status
Yana Studio Desktop workspace: files, editor, terminals, chat, tasks and a design canvas for a real project.
Runtime yana-rt Rust engine with one turn loop and one authority contract for every client and every provider.
Governance Capability manifests, human approval, hash-chained audit log, core-lock integrity.
Giám Thị Watcher outside any AI session that halts every later tool call when it finds drift.
Harness adapters Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Antigravity. Enforcement strength differs per host.
Knowledge layer Agents, skills, commands and rules that teach agents how to work. They grant no permissions.
Yana OS Local management plane: agent identity, autonomy levels, quotas, health, quarantine.
Yana Desktop / Web Earlier Electron shell and web UI. Studio is a separate rebuild, not a reskin.
Yana Wheelbot Robotics platform on ESP32-S3, in its own repository.

Live means shipped and in use. In development means real code exists but is not feature-complete. Experimental means opt-in and not independently verified.

yana-rt has 40 subcommands. Zero Python dependency. This is the source-defined count across feature builds, including feature-gated ones.

core/
├── hooks/    # 66 PreToolUse / PostToolUse / Stop hooks (63 shell, 3 JavaScript)
├── rules/    # 71 rules, most are guidance the agent applies; hooks enforce a subset
├── agents/   # 100 specialist agents
├── skills/   # 2,026 skills
├── commands/ # 170 Claude Code slash commands
└── config/
    └── core-lock.json    # SHA-256 manifest — 287 core files pinned

Yana Studio

One window for the things you switch between when working with AI on a project. Studio talks to models only through yana-rt; the UI layer never calls a provider.

Area What you get
Files and editor Open a real folder, search filenames, edit with CodeMirror. Files up to 8 MiB are editable; larger ones open as read-only 256 KiB windows. Saves detect outside changes before overwriting.
Terminals Real PTY sessions in tabs, or a grid of up to 12.
Git Read-only status, worktrees and diffs. Stage and commit are deliberately not AI tools.
Chat Streamed through yana-rt, saved conversations, stop button, approval prompts, token usage.
Models All 19 providers plus a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint. A local manager detects 9Router, Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, TurboFieldfare and AirLLM. API keys reach Rust over stdin and are stored encrypted in the OS keystore, never in workspace files.
Tasks Backed by the real yana-rt task store. Marking done requires evidence, and blocked is computed by the runtime.
Design canvas Native canvas with 22 components, phone and desktop screens, layers, undo/redo and guarded AI proposals.
Governance telemetry What was allowed, what was blocked, and why.

Not built yet: device registry, agent sessions screen, mobile pairing, SSH/Docker execution, permission-lease UI, signed auto-update. Per-screen status lives in tools/yana-studio/SCREEN-STATUS.md.

Build Studio from source

Needs Node 24+ and a C++ toolchain for node-pty.

cd tools/yana-studio
npm ci && npm run rebuild
npm run stage:runtime -- /absolute/path/to/yana-rt
npm start

A single Rust binary owns the turn loop and the authority check for every client, so Studio, the CLI and MCP do not each reimplement permission logic.

  • Providers: anthropic, openai, gemini, groq, deepseek, openrouter, xai, novita, nvidia, minimax, glm, huggingface, 9router, kimi (cloud), and ollama, lmstudio, llamacpp, turbofieldfare, airllm (local). The canonical list is src/model/catalog.rs; a contract test keeps Studio in sync with it.
  • Failover: typed provider errors, fallback providers and credential-pool rotation.
  • State: SQLite session store with full-text search, per-profile state, crash recovery, and shadow-git checkpoints with rollback.
  • Capability tools: file read/patch, command execution under validation, MCP client over stdio, web.search through a checked HTTPS layer, and a read-only LSP client.
  • Optional features: mcp, lsp, pty-bridge, Discord remote adapter. They are off in the default build.

Remaining runtime work is tracked in CURRENT-MILESTONE.md: unifying every client on one capability executor, and testing local-model tool calling against a real local model rather than a mock.

Performance

Measured 2026-10-20 on an Apple M4 MacBook Air (16 GB RAM, macOS 27.2), yana-rt 1.5.1 release build at commit 986093f5, against this repository. Each figure is the mean of 3 runs (100 for startup, 50 for hooks). The Python column is the script that each Rust command replaces. The last column is the 2026-08-26 snapshot; full history and method are in BENCHMARK.md.

Path yana-rt Python Result Same output? 2026-08-26
Process startup 4.16 ms 4.21 ms
doctor 143 ms 415 ms Rust 2.9x faster Yes, 16 checks each (11 ok, 1 warn, 4 info) 255 ms, Rust ran 10 checks vs 16
ci check 5.8 ms 33 ms Rust 5.7x faster Yes, 5 warnings each 414 ms, Rust found 0 vs 3
scan core/skills 0.55 s 8.47 s Rust 15.5x faster Same files (1,791 vs 1,795) and top finding; scores differ (40 vs 0) 4.45 s
HALT check hook 5.4 ms 3.80 ms
Destructive-command guard 4.9 ms not measured
Memory and size yana-rt Python
Peak RSS, scan core/skills 17.7 MiB 26.5 MiB
Peak RSS, default full-repo scan 22.4 MiB 29.4 MiB
Release binary 18.2 MiB

Since August, doctor and ci check reached output parity with Python and both got faster. The release binary grew from about 14 MiB.

Warning

The default full-repo scan is not a like-for-like comparison yet. Rust covers 620 files and reported no findings in 0.36 s; Python covers 1,643 files and reported 9 critical SE002 findings in 6.14 s. That is a parity gap to close, not a 17x speedup. The token-budget guard was not re-measured: in a fresh worktree it exits early because its lock state is not initialised, so a timing would only measure the error path.

These are single-machine numbers. Linux and Windows are not measured.

Giám Thị

An independent watcher that runs outside any AI session, from the operating system's own scheduler (launchd on macOS, a systemd timer on Linux, Task Scheduler on Windows) every 6 hours.

  1. It compares the repo against a baseline commit a human approved, over the files that control enforcement: hook settings for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, CI workflows, core/rules, core/gates, core/hooks, core/scripts and src/guard.
  2. On drift it writes GIAMTHI_HALT.lock. A hook that runs first on every tool call then denies everything while the lock exists.
  3. Only a person deleting the lock clears it. Neither the hook, the watcher nor any environment variable can.

Manage it with yana-ai giamthi install | status | repair | uninstall. It is opt-in, and because it runs on a schedule there is a window of up to 6 hours between a change and the halt. Codex fires PreToolUse only for shell commands, so Yana also checks the lock on SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit for Codex.

Harness adapters

Host How governance is applied Enforcement
Claude Code Native hooks and rules in .claude/ Runtime blocking on every tool call, hash-chained audit
Codex AGENTS.md, .codex/ hooks, synced skills and agents (yana-ai install --engine codex) Project-scoped hooks
Cursor .cursorrules, .cursor/rules, a beforeShellExecution hook Shell commands screened; MCP tool calls are not covered
Antigravity .agent/rules/yana-ai.md Advisory only, not enforced at the shell

Details and switching commands: adapters/README.md. The 170 Claude Code slash commands (/plan, /verify, /code-review and others) live in core/commands/ and run inside a session.

What protects you, and where it stops

Protection What it does Where it stops
Audit log Hash-chained, so editing or deleting a line is detectable (core/scripts/verify-audit-chain.sh). Tamper-detectable, not tamper-proof.
Core-lock SHA-256 manifest detects changed, deleted or injected files in core/. Proves the tree matches the lock, not that a human reviewed it: whoever can edit core/ can regenerate the lock. Giám Thị is the independent check.
Human gate Force-push, publish, deploy and delete need confirmation in the current session. Earlier approval does not carry over.
Giám Thị Locks every later tool call on a finding until a person removes the lock. Opt-in and periodic, not instant.
Rules and hooks Hooks block at runtime. Most files in core/rules describe behaviour the agent applies to itself; only what a hook wires in is enforced. There is no code-signing pipeline.
Destructive guard guard-destructive.sh blocks rm -rf, force-push, DROP TABLE and similar. Matches command strings, not a full shell parse, so a crafted command can slip past.

Antigravity is advisory, Cursor does not screen MCP calls, and browser-only web deployments without the Rust runtime are not fully governed. Details: known limitations.

Versioning

Three axes, each with its own number and registry: the product (not distributed), yana-rt on crates.io, and the yana-ai Python package on PyPI. Apps under tools/ ship through GitHub Releases with their own tags (studio-v* for Studio). Current version numbers are left out of this page on purpose, since they go stale; the badges above read them live. See VERSIONING.md.

More

ARCHITECTURE.md · PHILOSOPHY.md · ROADMAP.md · CURRENT-MILESTONE.md · CHANGELOG.md · BENCHMARK.md · CONTRIBUTING.md · SECURITY.md · Acknowledgements · Lineage
